title: Unique ID Generation
subtitle: Watch several servers mint IDs at the same time, and see why a plain counter stops working and what replaces it.
learn: Why a database auto-increment counter becomes a bottleneck and breaks when you add shards
How UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 differ, and why random keys hurt database indexes
How a Snowflake ID packs time, machine and sequence into 64 bits
How a ticket server hands out ID ranges, and what happens when a clock jumps backward
What sortable IDs buy you, and what they leak

steps.title: Every row needs a name
steps.body: Every new order, message or user needs an ID that no other row will ever have, like a serial number. With one server, a simple counter is enough. But when many servers create rows at the same moment, who decides the next number? A good answer is unique, cheap to produce, and not a bottleneck or a single point of failure. The animation shows two servers that both need IDs right now.
steps.idea: An ID scheme is judged on uniqueness, speed, size, sortability, and whether it needs coordination.
steps.caption: Two servers both need IDs right now.

steps.title: Let the database count
steps.body: The simplest scheme is a database auto-increment column (a sequence). The app inserts a row and the database hands back 1001, then 1002, and so on. IDs are small (8 bytes), keep increasing (with occasional gaps), and never collide. Use a 64-bit column, because a 32-bit INT overflows at about 2.1 billion rows. The catch: every insert goes through one database, which is one hop for every ID. A single primary can only take so many writes (rule of thumb: about 10,000 inserts per second).
steps.idea: Auto-increment is correct and compact, but one counter means one choke point.
steps.caption: The single database hands out the next number.

steps.title: Add a second writer
steps.body: Traffic grows, so you split the data across two databases (shards), and each keeps its own counter. Now both hand out 1001. The moment you merge, export, or reference rows across shards, the IDs collide. You can patch it by giving shard 1 the odd numbers and shard 2 the even ones, but a third shard means changing the scheme. (The database box is drawn once but stands for two shards.)
steps.idea: A counter only works while exactly one thing owns it. Sharding breaks that ownership.
steps.caption: Two shards, two counters: both issue 1001, so merged rows clash.

steps.title: Roll the dice locally
steps.body: A UUIDv4 is a 128-bit ID in which 122 bits are random. Each server makes one on its own, with no coordination, millions per second. A collision is possible in theory but absurdly unlikely: after a billion IDs, the chance of any duplicate is around 1 in 10 quintillion. The price is size (16 bytes) and randomness. Random keys land all over the primary-key index (the sorted lookup structure for the table) instead of at one spot, so writes are scattered and slow.
steps.idea: UUIDv4 trades coordination for bigger size and index-unfriendly randomness.
steps.caption: Each server mints its own ID with no network call.

steps.title: Put time at the front
steps.body: UUIDv7 (standardized in RFC 9562, 2024) keeps the 128-bit shape but starts with a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, followed by about 74 bits of random and counter data. There is still no coordination, and IDs created later sort later. In a B-tree index (the usual sorted index), new keys land at the right edge, so the busy pages stay in memory and page splits are rare. Ordering is only millisecond-accurate, and anyone who sees the ID can read the timestamp.
steps.idea: UUIDv7 keeps UUID's no-coordination property and adds time ordering, which indexes love.
steps.caption: Time-prefixed keys append at the edge of the index.

steps.title: Time + machine + sequence
steps.body: A Snowflake-style ID fits in 64 bits: 1 unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom start date (about 69 years), 10 bits for the worker number (1,024 workers), and a 12-bit sequence. Within one millisecond a worker counts 0 to 4095, so one worker can issue 4,096,000 IDs per second. As long as each worker has a unique number, no two machines can make the same ID, and no network call is needed. In the diagram the generator is one box, but in practice it is a small library inside each app server with its own worker number. (Run as a separate service, it would add one hop.)
steps.idea: Snowflake splits the ID into fields, so uniqueness comes from who and when, not from a shared counter.
steps.caption: Each app's local generator (drawn once) builds a sortable 64-bit ID.

steps.title: The clock goes backward
steps.body: Snowflake depends on the wall clock. If a clock correction (an NTP step, a leap second or a VM resume) moves time backward, even by 20 ms, the generator may repeat a timestamp it already used and issue a duplicate ID. A safe generator remembers the last timestamp it used, and after a restart must not start before it, so persist it or wait out the difference. If the clock is behind, it waits or refuses instead of guessing. Worker numbers must also be unique: assign them by a coordinator or config, never randomly.
steps.idea: Time-based IDs are only as safe as the clock and the uniqueness of worker numbers.
steps.caption: The generator refuses to issue IDs until the clock recovers.

steps.title: Lease ranges of IDs
steps.body: A ticket server is a small dedicated service, historically a database table with auto-increment, that hands out numbers. Asking it for every ID would bring back the bottleneck. So each app asks for a block, say 1,000 IDs, and spends them locally. That is one hop per 1,000 IDs (0.001 per ID). Run two ticket servers, one issuing odd blocks and one even, so one can fail. IDs are small and mostly increasing. A crashed app loses its unused block, leaving harmless gaps.
steps.idea: Handing out ranges turns one coordination call into thousands of free local IDs.
steps.caption: App A leases a block of 1,000 IDs.

steps.title: Why sortable matters
steps.body: Sortable IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake, and to a lesser extent ticket blocks) allow cursor paging, such as WHERE id < last_seen ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 50, and keep inserts append-like. But order across machines is only approximate (same-millisecond ties, clock skew), so never treat it as true event order. IDs also leak creation time and volume. Counters and time-based IDs are guessable, so do not use them as secrets. Check access on every request, or expose a random public ID.
steps.idea: Sortable IDs make queries and indexes faster, but their order is approximate and creation time becomes visible.
steps.caption: Both servers append to the same edge of the index.

steps.title: Pick by constraint
steps.body: Use auto-increment for a single database where simplicity wins. Use UUIDv7 when you want no coordination and standard tooling. Use Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs when size and throughput matter and you can manage worker numbers and clocks. Use ticket servers (ID blocks) when you want small numeric IDs with rare coordination. On large indexed tables, prefer UUIDv7 over UUIDv4 as a primary key, unless you need order-free values.
steps.idea: Every scheme trades coordination, size, ordering and clock trust. Choose the one whose weakness you can live with.
steps.caption: Five schemes, one trade-off each.

quiz.q: Two database shards each auto-increment from 1, and you later merge their orders into one table. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since each row has its own timestamp
The IDs become random and unsortable
Both shards produced the same IDs, so rows collide
quiz.why: Each counter is independent, so both shards issue 1001, 1002 and so on. Merged rows have duplicate keys, which is why a shared counter does not survive sharding.

quiz.q: A Snowflake worker has a 12-bit sequence field and 1 ms timestamp resolution. What is the most IDs one worker can issue per second?
quiz.why: 12 bits gives 4,096 values per millisecond, and there are 1,000 ms in a second, so 4,096 × 1,000 = 4,096,000. The 10-bit worker field (1,024) only sets how many workers exist.

quiz.q: Why does inserting UUIDv7 keys usually perform better than UUIDv4 keys on a large B-tree primary-key index?
options: New v7 keys land near the end of the index, so writes stay on a few hot pages
UUIDv7 is generated by the database
quiz.why: The leading timestamp makes keys increase over time, so inserts append at the right edge. Random v4 keys land on arbitrary pages, causing cache misses and page splits. Both are 16 bytes.

quiz.q: A Snowflake generator notices the system clock is 20 ms behind the timestamp of the last ID it issued. What is the safest behavior?
options: Use the current clock anyway and hope the sequence differs
Wait or refuse until the clock passes the last timestamp used
Pick a new random worker number
Reset the sequence to zero and continue
quiz.why: Reusing an earlier millisecond risks repeating a timestamp, worker and sequence combination already issued, which would create a duplicate. Waiting for time to catch up preserves uniqueness.

quiz.q: A ticket server hands each app a block of 1,000 IDs. What is the main benefit?
options: No gaps even if an app crashes
quiz.why: Apps spend a leased block locally, so coordination happens once per block. A crashed app loses its unused block, leaving gaps, and block order is not true time order.

cheatsheet.def: A database counter. Small and ordered, but one writer owns it, so it caps throughput and breaks when you shard.
128 bits, 122 random. No coordination, collision odds negligible, but 16 bytes and random order that scatters index writes.
128 bits led by a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp plus random bits (RFC 9562). Time-sortable, index-friendly, no coordination.
64 bits: 41 time (ms), 10 worker, 12 sequence. About 4.1 million IDs per second per worker; needs unique worker numbers and sane clocks.
A small service that leases blocks of numbers to apps. Coordination happens once per block; run two with odd/even offsets for availability.
Roughly time-ordered: IDs sort by creation to within the clock and millisecond precision, not by exact event order across machines.
The system clock moving backward after a sync. Generators must remember the last timestamp and wait or refuse rather than reuse it.
Paging with WHERE id < cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n. Fast with sortable IDs, no OFFSET scans.
